stories.headline: Oil dips as US weighs strikes and Iran offers Hormuz terms
stories.question: Will the US strike Iran again, or will Iran reopen the Strait of Hormuz?
stories.dek: Neither had happened by 2 November. Iran says Hormuz could reopen within two days if the US meets its conditions. Secretary of State Marco Rubio says no strike decision has been made.

so_far.text: The Strait of Hormuz is the narrow sea lane out of the Gulf. The US and Iran have been at war, and US military action is now on hold. The US is also blockading Iranian ports. Ships in the strait are still being attacked. A Qatari gas tanker was hit on 30 October, and another vessel was struck on 1 November. Iran says ships that hit mines are using routes it considers unauthorised.

what_happened.text: On 31 October US President Donald Trump said the US still had to deal with one or two sites in Iran. One is Pickaxe Mountain, a suspected underground nuclear complex. Iran denies nuclear work there. On 1 November Trump said the war will end "very soon, one way or the other", by a deal or militarily. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said no decision on resuming military action has been made. Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Hormuz could fully reopen within two days if the US lifts its port blockade, releases frozen assets and waives oil sanctions. On 2 November Brent fell about 3%, to below $110.

steps.text: Oil prices reflect fear about future supply, so attacks on ships in a key sea lane matter to markets.
Iran has named three conditions: lift the US port blockade, release frozen assets and waive oil sanctions.
Araghchi says a plan with mediators could fully reopen Hormuz within two days if those conditions are met.
In Washington, Trump says the war ends soon by deal or militarily, while Rubio says no strike decision is made.
Iran's Supreme Leader and army warn any new attack would spread the war; Bloomberg reports Gulf states fear fiercer retaliation.

stories.headline: US midterms: Democrats favoured, but seven Senate races are toss-ups
stories.question: What is at stake in the 3 November US midterms, and which races decide Congress?
stories.dek: Democrats need three more House seats and four more Senate seats to take Congress. Forecasts favour them, but seven Senate races are close and some counts could take days.

so_far.text: Americans vote on 3 November 2026 in the midterms, the elections held halfway through a president's term. The vote decides who controls Congress, meaning the House of Representatives and the Senate. Republicans hold the Senate 53–47, and Vice President Vance breaks ties. In the House, Republicans hold 218 seats plus one independent, Democrats hold 214, and two seats are vacant. On 23 October the Justice Department sued Alaska's election office to stop certification of the Senate result if Democrat Mary Peltola wins. On 27 October President Trump offered a $1 million reward for voter-fraud tips.

what_happened.text: By 1 November more than 51 million Americans had voted early, up from the 18 million in earlier reports. These totals do not show how people voted. Late polls stay tight. YouGov polls on 1 November had Democrats ahead by one to five points in Kansas, Iowa, Texas, Michigan, Maine and Ohio. Nebraska was tied 49–49 with independent candidate Osborn. Trump held rallies over the weekend in states Republicans won before, which the BBC said shows how tight the contest is. First polls close at 6 p.m. Eastern on 3 November, about 04:30 IST on 4 November.

steps.text: A Democratic House majority would bring committee investigations and leverage over government funding, including money for the war with Iran.
In the House, Democrats need a net gain of three seats to reach 218, the number for a majority.
In the Senate they need four net gains, because a 50–50 tie goes to Republicans through Vice President Vance's vote.
So the seven toss-up Senate races, including Alaska, Texas, Ohio and Maine, decide whether Democrats reach that fourth seat.
A Democratic Senate would control confirmations of judges and Cabinet members, which is why that fourth seat matters so much.

stories.headline: North Korea-linked hackers steal $6.3 billion from Binance, FBI says
stories.question: How did hackers steal $6.3 billion from Binance, and are crypto users safe?
stories.dek: Binance says the attack involved a compromised laptop, and the FBI blames North Korea. Binance says it is paying for the loss itself, so customer balances are still backed.

so_far.text: Binance is a crypto exchange, a company where people buy, sell and store digital tokens. The FBI uses the label TraderTraitor for a North Korea-linked hacking operation. In February 2025, TraderTraitor was blamed for stealing $1.5 billion from Bybit, another exchange. The FBI now says the same operation was behind a theft at Binance. At $6.3 billion, the Binance theft is more than four times the size of the Bybit theft.

what_happened.text: On 29 October 2026, hackers stole tokens worth $6.3 billion from Binance, and Binance paused customer withdrawals. Co-CEO Richard Teng called it a "complex attack" involving a compromised laptop and malicious software meant to delete evidence. The FBI said North Korea was behind the theft, under the label TraderTraitor. It said it saw the hackers converting stolen tokens to Ethereum and preparing to launder them. By 1 November, Binance said it had replaced 90% of the stolen value by buying new tokens with company money. It expected to reopen withdrawals on Sunday, 1 November.

steps.text: Binance says the attack involved a compromised laptop and malicious software meant to delete evidence of the activity.
Software that deletes evidence makes it harder for investigators to work out exactly how the attackers got in.
The FBI says the hackers converted stolen tokens to Ethereum and were preparing to launder them, which means hiding where money came from.
The FBI published addresses to watch and urged service providers to block related transactions, to make that laundering harder.
Binance bought replacement tokens with its own money, so it says customer balances are still backed at least one-to-one.

stories.headline: Nature summit agrees Yerevan Pathway, but leaves money questions open
stories.question: What did COP17's Yerevan Pathway agree, and can it save the 2030 nature targets?
stories.dek: Countries agreed priorities to 2030, including phasing out nature-harmful subsidies and more money for poorer nations. But the world is off track, pledges are small, and big finance decisions moved to 2028.

so_far.text: The Kunming-Montreal framework is the world's shared plan to protect nature. It sets 23 targets for 2030. One is "30x30": protecting 30% of land and 30% of oceans. Rich countries also promised money to developing countries, but they missed their goal of $20 billion a year by 2025. A first global review then checked progress. It found the world off track, with fewer than half of national targets on track. COP17, the summit of countries in the UN Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD), opened in Yerevan on 19 October 2026.

what_happened.text: On 31 October 2026, COP17 adopted the Yerevan Pathway at its closing session, after talks ran about 24 hours past schedule. The Pathway sets priorities to 2030: phasing out subsidies that harm nature, more finance, science and technical support for developing countries, aligning budgets with the framework, and stronger monitoring and review. Countries announced nearly $2 billion in new funding. Criteria for a finance system after 2030 were agreed. But whether it will be a new fund or existing arrangements was put off to COP18 in Ecuador in 2028. Decisions on the Cali Fund's design were also deferred two years.

steps.text: Protecting nature costs money, and the yearly funding shortfall is estimated at about $700 billion.
Among its 2030 priorities, the Pathway lists phasing out nature-harmful subsidies and more finance for developing countries.
The Pathway lists these fixes, but each government must still change its own budgets and rules at home.
Rich and emerging countries did not agree who should pay, so the finance decision moved to 2028.
That leaves about two years before the 2030 deadline, while fewer than half of national targets are on track.

analogy.breaks: A family can enforce its own plan. Countries cannot force each other to pay or to act.

items.view: The outcome was 'not commensurate' with the crisis.
The outcome was a step forward, but weak on harmful subsidies.
The test is what governments change at home, not what they agreed in Yerevan.

for_you.text: The direct effect on your prices or EMIs is small. India has its own 23 national biodiversity targets. Environment Minister Bhupender Yadav used COP17 to call for predictable global finance. One report says India, with China and Saudi Arabia, may be discussed as a future funder. It does not say India agreed or refused. The finance system is due to be decided at COP18 in 2028.

next.text: Watch COP18 in Ecuador in 2028, where countries decide the post-2030 finance system. Before then, countries can signal voluntary contributions in confidential talks. CBD chief Astrid Schomaker says the real test is what governments change at home.

sections.title: World
sections.gist: Ukraine's local truce held while Russian strikes continued elsewhere, Israel's officials say the election result stands, and France faces a 5 November strike.

items.headline: Ukraine's six-day Oleshky truce ends quietly; US weighs Black Sea truce
items.text: A six-day local ceasefire in Oleshky, in Ukraine's Kherson region, ended on the night of 1 November. The US helped arrange it, and no violations were reported. Russian airstrikes went on in other parts of Ukraine during that time. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said interest is growing in a limited ceasefire in the Black Sea. He said the US is studying proposals from Turkey and India. Separately, the Wall Street Journal reported that the US is pushing to restore Russian gas sales to Europe through Ukraine. It is not yet known whether a Black Sea truce will follow, or what it would cover.
items.background: The US is trying small, local truces in the Russia-Ukraine war because a full ceasefire has not been agreed.
items.why: India is one of two countries whose Black Sea truce proposals Washington says it is reviewing.

items.headline: Israeli officials say vote stands after Netanyahu's 'stolen' claim
items.text: Israeli officials said the results of the country's election will stand. AP News reported this on 1 November. The officials spoke after Netanyahu claimed that Arabs stole the vote. The report does not say which officials spoke. It also does not say what evidence, if any, backed the claim. In most democracies, official election bodies count and certify the votes. A politician's claim alone does not change a certified result. It is not yet known whether Netanyahu will press the claim further.
items.background: Israel recently held a national election. Netanyahu has questioned the outcome, claiming that Arabs stole the vote.
items.why: When officials reject a leader's claim that a vote was stolen, it signals the count is not being reopened.

items.headline: Over 300,000 march across France; day ends in clashes
items.text: More than 300,000 people marched across France on 31 October, the New York Times reported. Some wore Halloween costumes. The Guardian said the protests were largely peaceful. The day still ended in violence, as police clashed with masked rioters. The New York Times said the clashes had erupted again. So this was not the first time such a day ended in violence. The sources do not say why people marched or how many were arrested. It is not yet known when the next protest day will be.
items.background: France has seen repeated days of street protest that ended in clashes; 31 October was the latest.
items.why: Clashes keep following mostly peaceful marches, so the tension in France has not eased. The sources report no direct effect on India.

sections.title: India
sections.gist: Five Kuki men were killed in Manipur, and two foreign guests died in a suspected electrocution at a Bengaluru hotel pool.

items.headline: Five Kuki men killed in two incidents in Manipur
items.text: Police in Manipur said on 1 November that five people had been killed in two separate incidents. On 31 October, three Kuki men died in a gunfight in Noney district. Separately, two Kuki men who had gone missing were found dead in Kangpokpi district. Finding the two bodies set off protests in Kangpokpi, and demonstrators clashed with each other. The main Kuki organisation blamed Naga separatist groups for the killings. The reports did not give details of the security response. It is not yet known who carried out the killings, or whether arrests have been made.
items.background: Manipur, a state in India's north-east, has seen repeated violence between ethnic communities. Kukis and Nagas are two of its tribal communities.
items.why: Fresh killings and street clashes show Manipur's conflict is still unsettled, with risk of further violence.

items.headline: Two foreign guests die in suspected electrocution at Bengaluru hotel pool
items.text: Two foreign guests died on 30 October in the swimming pool of the Conrad, a five-star hotel in Bengaluru. Police suspect electrocution. One was a German crew member of the airline Lufthansa. The other was a Slovak project manager working for IBM. Police filed an FIR, the first formal police complaint, against the hotel management. It is under Section 106 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, which covers causing death by negligence. Investigators are checking the pool's lighting wiring, its pump and its earthing. Earthing is the wire that carries stray current safely into the ground. The findings have not yet been made public.
items.background: A faulty light, pump or missing earthing can leak electric current into pool water, which conducts it to swimmers.
items.why: The case raises questions about how electrical safety in Indian hotels and public pools is checked and enforced.

items.headline: Cyclone Murasu heads for Andhra coast days after Cyclone Arnab
items.text: Cyclone Murasu is expected to cross the coast near Ongole, between Nellore and Narsapur. Landfall is expected between about 11:30 pm IST on 2 November and 4 am on 3 November 2026, as a severe cyclonic storm. The India Meteorological Department (IMD), the national weather agency, expects winds of 100–110 km/h, with gusts up to 120 km/h. About 2,000 people had been moved from low-lying coastal areas by 2 November. The state disaster authority plans to move about 30,000. Six NDRF and seven SDRF rescue teams are deployed. Schools are shut in Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu and Odisha.
items.background: On 28 October 2026, Cyclone Arnab struck the Andhra Pradesh coast.
items.why: If you live in or have family in Nellore, Prakasam, Bapatla or Krishna districts, these districts are on alert.

items.headline: INDIA bloc rallies in Delhi to demand Chief Election Commissioner's removal
items.text: On 1 November 2026 the INDIA bloc, an alliance of opposition parties, held its 'Vote Bachao, Desh Bachao' rally at Ramlila Maidan in Delhi. It followed a march from Minto Road. Leaders demanded Kumar's removal. Rahul Gandhi, Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha, alleged 'vote theft' in several states and in the 2024 Lok Sabha polls. He said Kumar 'will be sent to jail' for 'treason'. Akhilesh Yadav said West Bengal was 'stolen through SIR and force'. The BJP called the crowd 'empty chairs'. Delhi Police had allowed the rally but not a march from Connaught Place.
items.background: The Election Commission (EC) runs India's elections and keeps the voter lists.
items.why: If you vote, this fight is about whose names stay on the voter list.

sections.title: Your money & life
sections.gist: Fuel costs rise for restaurants and airlines, Delhi's pollution curbs begin, and UPI and GST both hit big October numbers.

items.headline: Commercial LPG up ₹10; jet fuel rises for fourth month
items.text: Commercial LPG cylinders cost more from 1 November. The 19-kg cylinder rose by ₹10 to ₹2,820. That is a rise of about a third of one per cent. Aviation turbine fuel (ATF), the fuel jet planes burn, rose by ₹1.37 per litre. It now costs ₹138.5 per litre. ATF has now gone up four months in a row. IndiGo's CEO warned that jet fuel costs will stay high. The CEO asked for lower taxes and airport charges. It is not yet known whether the government will act on that request.
items.background: Commercial LPG is the larger 19-kg gas cylinder. ATF is the fuel airlines buy. Both prices changed on 1 November.
items.why: Fuel is a major cost for airlines. Four monthly rises in a row, which IndiGo's CEO expects to continue, can push up air fares.

items.headline: Delhi's winter pollution curbs begin, with 50% work from home
items.text: Delhi's winter pollution plan began on 1 November. Older vehicles that meet only the BS-IV emission standard are barred. BS-IV is an older standard, so these vehicles pollute more than newer ones. Construction is restricted, and 50% of staff are to work from home. Commuters from Noida, Gurugram and Ghaziabad now need to check whether their car or bike may enter Delhi. The curbs start even though October's air quality index (AQI), a daily pollution score, was at an eight-year low, India Today reports. The sources do not say how long the curbs will last.
items.background: Delhi's air usually gets worst in winter, when cold, still air traps smoke and dust near the ground.
items.why: If you live or work in Delhi-NCR, these rules decide whether you can drive in and where you work.

items.headline: UPI crosses 25 billion payments in a month for the first time
items.text: UPI, India's instant phone-payment system, handled more than 25 billion transactions in October. Fortune India reported on 2 November that this is the first month to cross that mark. The payments were worth ₹31.53 lakh crore. That works out to more than 80 crore payments a day on average. The average payment was about ₹1,260 or less. ET Retail said festive spending drove the record. The facts do not give any figures for November. They also do not mention any change in UPI charges.
items.background: UPI lets you pay straight from your bank account through a phone app, by scanning a QR code or entering an ID.
items.why: The record shows how much of India's everyday spending now runs through UPI on phones.

items.headline: GST collections rise 22.9% to ₹2.31 lakh crore in October
items.text: Gross GST collections rose 22.9% to ₹2.31 lakh crore in October, ET CFO reported on 2 November. Gross means everything collected. Net means what is left after refunds to businesses. Net GST revenue rose 25.6% to ₹2.03 lakh crore. A 22.9% rise means gross collections a year earlier were roughly ₹1.88 lakh crore. So this October brought in about ₹43,000 crore more. The facts do not say what drove the rise. The next monthly figures will show whether this pace holds.
items.background: GST, the goods and services tax, is built into the price of most things you buy. Collections are reported every month.
items.why: GST is the tax you pay on most purchases, so its collections show how much tax the government earns from spending.

sections.title: Markets & money
sections.gist: Reliance jumps on 41% profit growth, factory growth eases, the RBI spends $55 billion defending the rupee, and SEBI pitches tax relief.

items.headline: Reliance shares jump nearly 7.5% as quarterly profit rises 41%
items.text: Reliance Industries shares surged nearly 7.5% on 2 November after its quarterly results. These cover July to September, the second quarter of financial year 2026–27. Net profit rose 41% from a year earlier to ₹25,548 crore. Revenue rose 29% to ₹3.32 lakh crore. That is about ₹7.70 of profit for every ₹100 of sales. Separately, Jio said mobile tariff hikes can wait. It also said it is looking for 10–15 partners for its business abroad. It is not yet known when Jio might raise tariffs.
items.background: Reliance Industries is one of India's biggest companies, and its businesses include Jio, the mobile network.
items.why: Jio says tariff hikes can wait, which matters to its mobile users. Reliance's share price affects many Indian investors.

items.headline: Factory growth slows slightly in October, PMI shows
items.text: The HSBC India Manufacturing PMI fell to 54.7 in October from 55.1 in September. The PMI (Purchasing Managers' Index) is a monthly survey of factory managers. A reading above 50 means activity is growing; below 50 means it is shrinking. So factories are still growing, just a little more slowly. The Hindu reports that output and new orders rose more softly. The reading stays above its long-run average and well above the 50 mark. November's survey will show whether the slowdown continues.
items.background: The PMI is one of the earliest monthly signals of how India's factories are doing, released before official output data.
items.why: Factory activity drives jobs and incomes; a small dip from a high level is not a contraction.

items.headline: RBI's dollar holdings fall $55 billion while defending the rupee
items.text: The RBI's foreign currency assets fell by $55 billion over seven weeks, Mumbai Mirror reported on 1 November. That is close to $8 billion a week on average. The RBI sold dollars to defend the rupee. Here is how it works. When many people want dollars, the rupee weakens. The RBI sells dollars from its reserves and takes rupees in return. That extra supply of dollars slows the rupee's fall. The source does not say how large the remaining reserves are. So it is not yet known how long the RBI can keep this up.
items.background: The RBI holds a large stock of foreign currency, mostly dollars, partly to steady the rupee in rough times.
items.why: A weaker rupee makes imports like fuel and electronics, foreign travel and studying abroad more expensive.

items.headline: SEBI proposes scrapping long-term capital gains tax for foreign investors
items.text: SEBI, India's market regulator, has proposed scrapping long-term capital gains (LTCG) tax for foreign investors. LTCG tax is the tax on profit from investments held for a long period. SEBI also suggested tax relief for mutual fund investors. Under it, Indian investors would not pay LTCG when they sell existing fund holdings to buy new ones, sources told Mint. SEBI says high capital gains taxes and transaction costs are deterring investors. These are only recommendations. The government decides whether to accept them, likely in the Union Budget in February 2027.
items.background: Tax rules are set by the government through the Budget and tax laws, not by SEBI.
items.why: If accepted, switching between mutual funds could become cheaper for Indian investors; nothing changes for now.

items.headline: Bank of England expected to raise interest rates to 4%
items.text: The Bank of England is expected to raise interest rates at its early-November meeting, Reuters reported on 2 November. The Financial Times says the rate is set to rise to 4%, to bring down inflation. Raising rates makes borrowing costlier, which cools spending and slows price rises. Reuters says the Bank may also push back on market bets that more increases will follow. The size of any future moves is not yet known.
items.background: The Bank of England is the UK's central bank; like the RBI, it sets the country's main interest rate.
items.why: No direct effect on Indian prices or EMIs; it shows inflation pressure in big economies is still pushing rates up.

sections.title: Science, health & climate
sections.gist: ISRO adds a NavIC satellite and eyes a 2027 Tamil Nadu launch. A UN report warns of lasting ice loss.

items.headline: ISRO launches NVS-03; new Tamil Nadu spaceport eyes 2027 debut
items.text: ISRO has launched NVS-03, a new navigation satellite for NavIC. Prime Minister Narendra Modi praised the scientists after the launch, in reports on 31 October. ISRO Chairman V. Narayanan said two more navigation satellites will follow to strengthen the NavIC constellation, the group of satellites that work together. He also said the first rocket launch from the new Kulasekarapattinam spaceport in Tamil Nadu is likely in March–April 2027. That would give ISRO a second launch site. Dates for the next two NavIC satellites have not been given.
items.background: NavIC is India's own satellite navigation system. It works like GPS, but India runs it, and it covers India and the region around it.
items.why: More NavIC satellites mean India relies less on foreign navigation systems for maps, transport and defence.

items.headline: UN-backed report: even a brief overshoot of 1.5C harms ice
items.text: A UN-backed report, covered by The Guardian on 2 November, looks at overshooting the Paris agreement's 1.5C warming target. Overshoot means global temperature rises above the target for a while, then comes back down. The report finds even a temporary overshoot could cause lasting harm to glaciers and polar ice sheets. It calls some overshoot inevitable. So it says global heating should then be brought back below 1C. That is a third lower than the 1.5C target itself. The facts do not say how or when that could be done.
items.background: The Paris agreement is the global climate deal. 1.5C is its target limit for global warming.
items.why: Missing the 1.5C goal even for a while could cause lasting damage to the world's ice.

items.headline: Washington reports second human bird flu case from dairy
items.text: On 1 November, Yakima County in Washington state, US, reported its second human case of H5N1 bird flu. The patient had been exposed at a dairy with infected cattle. They are in hospital with severe illness and have other health conditions. As of 29 October, 33 dairy herds in the county had tested positive for H5N1. Officials say there is no evidence of the virus spreading from person to person. They are watching the patient's close contacts for symptoms.
items.background: H5N1 is a bird flu virus. It has spread to US dairy cattle, and people working closely with infected animals can catch it.
items.why: Person-to-person spread is what would make bird flu a global threat. So far, officials report none. No direct effect on India.

sections.title: Formula 1
sections.gist: Kimi Antonelli, 20, is F1's youngest champion. Verstappen wins in Mexico, and Middle East tensions put the Gulf races in doubt.

items.headline: Antonelli, 20, becomes F1's youngest champion; Verstappen wins Mexico
items.text: At the Mexico City Grand Prix on 1 November, Kimi Antonelli became Formula 1's youngest world champion. The Italian finished third, aged 20 years and 68 days. He won the title without winning the race. Max Verstappen won for Red Bull, ahead of Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton. Verstappen took control during the race's only pitstop, on lap 28 of 71. The win lifted him to second in the standings. Hamilton said a first-lap clash with his Ferrari team-mate Charles Leclerc cost Ferrari the win. He called for 'serious talks' inside the team. It is not yet known how Ferrari will respond.
items.background: A driver becomes champion once no rival can catch his points total, even with races still left.
items.why: Antonelli now holds the record as F1's youngest champion. Ferrari's two drivers are in an open dispute.

items.headline: Yamaha skips MotoGP's Qatar race; F1 says it will still race
items.text: On 1 November Yamaha said it would skip MotoGP's Qatar Grand Prix, due the following week. It is the first manufacturer to say so publicly. Yamaha cited company-wide travel restrictions after assessing the Middle East crisis. Riders had also raised concerns. Formula 1 says it still intends to race in Qatar on 27–29 November, and in Abu Dhabi. F1 says travel advice and insurance cover have not changed since May. It also says safety comes first. Imola, a circuit in Italy, is preparing as a backup venue. It is not yet known whether other MotoGP teams will follow Yamaha.
items.background: MotoGP is motorcycle racing's top series. Both MotoGP and Formula 1 hold late-season races in the Middle East.
items.why: The Middle East crisis is now affecting global sport. F1's own Qatar race is due on 27–29 November.

sections.title: Cricket — the masala
sections.gist: India win the New Zealand T20 series 3-2 despite two late losses. An injury-hit New Zealand side now faces Rohit and Kohli in the ODIs.

items.headline: India take T20I series 3-2 as New Zealand win final game
items.text: India won the five-match T20I series in New Zealand 3-2. They had led 3-0, but New Zealand won the last two games. New Zealand won the fifth T20I in Hamilton by seven wickets. Tim Seifert and Glenn Phillips powered the chase. Earlier, Milne dismissed Abhishek Sharma and Sanju Samson in successive overs during the powerplay. The powerplay is the first six overs, when fielding limits apply. Ishan Kishan and Shreyas Iyer then added 93 runs off 43 balls. That is about 13 runs an over. India still could not post enough to win.
items.background: A T20I is an international match of 20 overs per side. India played five of them in New Zealand.
items.why: India won the series, but New Zealand fought back to win the last two games after trailing 3-0.

items.headline: Ravindra and Chapman injured, miss New Zealand's ODIs against India
items.text: New Zealand will be without Rachin Ravindra and Mark Chapman for the ODI series against India. ODIs are one-day internationals of 50 overs per side. The Hindu reported New Zealand's cricket board as saying that neither player recovered from injury in time. Tim Seifert is now in the squad for the entire series. Henry Nicholls comes in for the first three games. Foxcroft comes in for the last two. So New Zealand's squad will change partway through the series. The facts do not give India's squad or the match dates.
items.background: India and New Zealand are due to play an ODI series, and New Zealand has now named its squad.
items.why: With two injured players out, India will face a weaker New Zealand side than New Zealand would have chosen.

Prices fell even though strikes were still being weighed and ships were still being hit
The US had accepted Iran's two-day plan

quiz.q: Suppose Democrats take exactly three Senate seats from Republicans and lose none. Who controls the Senate?

Republicans, because Vice President Vance breaks the 50–50 tie
Nobody, until a new election is held
quiz.why: Three gains leave a 50–50 split. Vance's tie-breaking vote keeps Republicans in control, so Democrats need a net gain of four.

Binance bought replacement tokens with its own money
Hackers returned most of the funds
